segments.text: Hello.
Day twenty-seven.
Today's session is one I hope you never need.
We're going to make a plan for a slip.
Not because I expect one.
Because the best time to plan for a hard moment is on a calm day, well before it comes.
Let me say the true things plainly.
If you ever do have one, a slip doesn't undo anything.
The most useful thing is to get straight back to your plan, right now, not tomorrow.
A slip does make the next one more likely, which is why the next hour matters.
Most people who quit for good had slips, or several tries, along the way.
So a slip wouldn't make you unusual.
And it wouldn't erase a single day you've done.
The danger was never the one.
It's the thought that comes straight after it.
You know this passenger by now.
It says, "Well, that's it.
You've blown it.
You might as well carry on."
That thought is the whole risk.
So that's what the plan is for.
Let's walk through it once, so it's familiar.
Take a breath, in a way that feels comfortable for you.
Imagine it's happened.
You've had a few puffs.
Notice what shows up.
Disappointment, maybe.
That passenger, starting to talk.
Let it be there.
Now, the plan.
First, stop where you are.
Put it down.
Step away from where you're standing.
Second, one slow breath out.
Third, open DayXero and log it.
There's a short track there for exactly this moment.
One minute, and it walks you through the rest.
And fourth, ask one question.
Not "what's wrong with me."
Just, "what set this off?"
Then the very next choice is yours again.
That's all.
In a moment, you'll write down your own first step, in your own words, and who you'd tell.
Then put the plan away.
You've come twenty-seven days without it.
It isn't a prediction.
It's a fire extinguisher.
Most people who own one never use it, and sleep better anyway.
The plan is there.
And you're still here.
I'll see you in a few days.
